198.text:
Marta took the heavier blade off the rail herself, slid it through her belt at the hip, and gave the smith a nod that needed no words. He went back inside; the hammer started up again before they'd cleared the gate, the village's morning heartbeat behind them.

The quarry track ran uphill through thin pine, dew steaming off it where the first light caught. Marta walked like a woman who'd hauled stone all her life—unhurried, steady, the shield riding easy on her arm—and she talked the way she'd talked in the forge, low and twice over.

"Five of them at the camp, he says, and drag marks going past. So we go quiet up to the rocks and we look before we look at anything else. If they're sitting out front, we decide there, not down the hill with our blood up. And if there's a bundle in that camp—" her jaw worked once— "then we do it smart, because a tied-up man doesn't get smarter by us being stupid. That's what I'm saying."

The trees thinned. The quarry opened out ahead, gray and terraced, its cut benches stacked up the hillside like the steps of something enormous, and the warren mouth showed where it always had—a black fold in the rock at the base of the lower cut, the spoil heap before it trodden and pocked with the prints they remembered. Smoke stood thin and straight above it. A morning cook-fire.

They came off the track into the pine edge and Marta put her back against a trunk, breathing through her nose, listening. The shield came around off her shoulder into her left hand without hurry. From the rocks, at this distance, the camp was a smear of hides and fire-glow against the black mouth, and something small moved between the tents—two of them, then one again.

"There's your first light," she murmured. "How do you want to go at it—up the rocks on the left where the ground hides us, or straight down and be seen?"

200.text:
"Then we go slow and we go quiet," Marta breathed, and moved off through the pines with her shield hugged close to her chest so the rim couldn't flash.

The left-hand rocks were old quarry waste, tumbled slabs furred with moss, and they gave handholds enough. Marta went first where the going was sure and waved him up where it wasn't, and twice she stopped with one knee on stone and just listened—once when a jay went off somewhere below, once for nothing either of them could name. The camp sounds came up to them as they climbed: a log knocked, a thin high voice scolding another, the small domestic noise of a fire being fed.

The top slab gave a ledge behind a shoulder of rock, and Marta bellied onto it and made room beside her. From there the whole camp lay below, close enough to smell—wet hide, smoke, and something sourer underneath.

Two goblins by the fire, one turning a spit with a rabbit-sized thing on it, the other picking at its feet with a bone. A third sat against a tent of stitched hides, asleep or near it, a crude shortbow across its knees. That was three.

The fourth was easier to find than to look at. It came out of the larger tent hauling on a rope, and the rope came out after it—and the rope was tied around the ankles of a man.

Trud. Alive. His hands were bound in front of him, his mouth a dark rag-knot, and he moved like a man four days beaten—slow, careful, dragged a body-length at a time toward the midden at the camp's edge while his keeper idled the rope and looked the other way.

Marta's breath went out through her teeth, slow and even, controlled the way a bellows is controlled. Her free hand found Alaric's sleeve and squeezed once, hard.

"Four awake, one sleeping," she whispered, barely a shape of sound. "One's got him on a rope. If we take the roper quiet, the other two are thirty paces off with their backs half turned." Her eyes cut to him. "But the moment he cries out—or the rope pulls wrong—it's all of it at once. So. Quiet, or loud?"
